title: Visa Delays Are Killing Startups Across the US, UK and Canada — Here's What Founders Can Do
excerpt: From a $100,000 H-1B fee in the US to 10-year waits in Canada, immigrant entrepreneurs face an increasingly hostile global visa landscape. Experts say treating immigration as strategy, not paperwork, is the only way forward.
body:
• The US immigration system delayed 150,000 businesses and 500,000 jobs between 2013 and 2021, according to a Pioneer Institute study, with Indian and Mexican applicants facing decade-long green card waits.
  • A new $100,000 fee on certain H-1B cases and a shift to wage-weighted lottery selection are making the US visa pathway more expensive and selective for founders in 2026.
  • Canada's once-popular Start-up Visa programme now has a backlog of 43,200 applicants, with estimated wait times stretching beyond 10 years — up from 18 months originally.
  • Immigration attorneys recommend a portfolio approach: combining O-1, L-1, E-2, and early Green Card strategies rather than relying on a single visa pathway.

When Gaurav Chauhan moved from India to Canada in 2022 under the country's Start-up Visa (SUV) programme, the processing time was around 18 months. Three years later, his co-founder Amit's permanent residency file is still pending, and the official wait tracker now shows more than 10 years.

"It feels like living in a sweet jail," Chauhan told Livemint. "You can see everything Canada offers — but you're constantly waiting for someone to decide if you can stay."

Chauhan's story is not an outlier. Across the three countries where Indian-origin founders most commonly build businesses — the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada — visa systems are buckling under bureaucratic weight, policy whiplash, and surging demand. The result is an accelerating crisis that forces entrepreneurs to choose between their companies and their immigration status.

The US: 150,000 Businesses Delayed, New Barriers Rising

A Pioneer Institute study found that the US immigration system delayed the creation of roughly 150,000 businesses and 500,000 jobs between 2013 and 2021. With more than 180 visa categories and a 99 percent rejection rate for immigrant visa applications, the system remains what University of Wisconsin-Superior Professor Joshua Bedi calls "Kafka-esque."

https://x.com/Halosznn_/status/2079921411997462899

"Our competitors are streamlining their immigration processes to attract top talent. If the U.S. doesn't modernize its system, we risk losing the next generation of innovators and entrepreneurs."

— Professor Joshua Bedi, University of Wisconsin-Superior

The landscape has only tightened in 2026. A presidential proclamation in September 2025 introduced a one-time $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B cases involving overseas entry. The Department of Homeland Security has also moved from a purely random H-1B lottery to a weighted selection process favouring higher-paid, higher-skilled registrants, effective February 2026.

Meanwhile, proposed changes to student visa rules threaten to shrink another pipeline. The DHS has proposed eliminating the "Duration of Status" framework for F-1 visas, replacing it with fixed four-year admission periods. Danielle Goldman, CEO of immigration firm Build, warned that thousands of Indian professionals in AI, machine learning, and data science could face uncertainty if the changes are implemented.

Canada: From 18 Months to a Decade

Canada's SUV programme, launched in 2013, once promised a quick path from idea to permanent residency. It became especially popular with Indian entrepreneurs for its combination of PR access, family inclusion, and a fast-tracked citizenship timeline.

But the programme has been overwhelmed. As of late 2025, approximately 43,200 applicants were stuck in the SUV queue, according to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). Processing times have ballooned from the advertised 12-18 months to over a decade. Ottawa capped the number of support letters per incubator at 10 per year in 2024, acknowledging that "paper businesses" — ventures created solely to secure immigration paperwork — had flooded the system.

Nishant Ahlawat, a former SUV applicant turned immigration lawyer in Toronto, no longer recommends the programme. "No serious entrepreneur is going to wait a decade for residency," he told Livemint. Some founders, like food-tech entrepreneur Maulik Pandya, have given up entirely. His LinkedIn post about leaving Canada went viral, capturing the frustration of hundreds caught in limbo.

The UK: Expensive and Unwelcoming

Britain's challenges are different in character but similar in effect. Upfront visa costs for skilled workers are ten times the international average, according to the Royal Society — £12,451 for a five-year visa, including NHS surcharges and sponsorship fees. For startups that cannot match the salary packages of firms like Google or Anthropic, these costs are prohibitive.

Skilled worker visa applications fell 39 percent in the year to June 2026, the Times reported. The Global Talent Fund, launched to attract 60 to 80 top researchers, has brought in just 18. Tech founders say the system makes the UK "feel unwelcoming," even as some of its biggest tech companies — Wayve ($24 billion), ElevenLabs, Synthesia — were founded by immigrants who originally came for British universities.

What Founders Should Do Now

Immigration attorney Muhammed Uzum, writing in Inc., argues that 2026 is the year founders must stop treating immigration as paperwork and start treating it as strategy. Rather than betting on a single visa, he recommends a portfolio approach.

For founders with demonstrated impact, the O-1 "extraordinary ability" visa remains powerful. USCIS guidance now recognises that a founder's own company can petition for them under certain structures. For those with overseas operations, the L-1 intracompany transfer can serve as an expansion pathway. Founders from treaty countries can pursue the E-2 investor visa, which can be obtained relatively quickly when the business is operational.

"The most underestimated move for 2026 is starting the Green Card strategy earlier than many companies historically did."

— Muhammed Uzum, immigration attorney, writing in Inc.

The EB-2 National Interest Waiver and EB-1 extraordinary ability categories allow founders to apply for permanent residency without an employer sponsor — a critical advantage for entrepreneurs. But building the evidence base requires documentation of market traction, investment, patents, and job creation from the start, not as a last-minute scramble.

For Indian founders specifically, the stakes are compounded by the green card backlog. Indian and Mexican applicants have historically waited nearly a decade for permanent residency, compared to four years on average. With immigrants 80 percent more likely to start businesses than US-born citizens, and nearly two-thirds of US AI firms having immigrant founders, the delays carry economic consequences that extend far beyond individual companies.

What's Next

Canada is preparing its next immigration levels plan, which will determine whether the SUV backlog can be cleared. In the US, the proposed student visa changes face a public comment period before any implementation. In the UK, the government has promised further reforms to high-skilled immigration routes later this year.

But for founders navigating the system today, the advice from experts is consistent: plan early, diversify visa strategies, build evidence continuously, and treat travel decisions as operational risks. The countries competing for entrepreneurial talent have not stopped wanting it. They have just made it much harder to get in.
